paragraphs.heading: America's first station
paragraphs.text: Skylab was the first space station the United States launched, run by NASA. Between May 1973 and February 1974, astronauts lived aboard for about 24 weeks, in three crews of three called Skylab 2, Skylab 3 and Skylab 4. It was the world's second station, after the Soviet Salyut 1. Work aboard included an orbital workshop, a solar observatory, watching Earth, ten spacewalks and hundreds of experiments.

paragraphs.heading: Made from a rocket stage
paragraphs.text: Skylab grew out of the Apollo Applications Program. Its body was the third stage of a Saturn V, the S-IVB, repurposed and set up as a dry workshop that took the stage's place at launch. A Saturn V carried it into low Earth orbit with no one aboard, the last flight of the rocket best known for the Apollo Moon landings. Three later missions brought crews of three in Apollo command and service modules on the smaller Saturn IB. With one of those modules docked, the station's mass was 90,610 kg.

paragraphs.heading: Inside the station
paragraphs.text: Skylab's parts included a multi-spectral solar observatory called the Apollo Telescope Mount, a docking adapter with two ports, an airlock with hatches for spacewalks and the orbital workshop, the main living space. Power came from solar arrays and from fuel cells in the docked Apollo craft. At the back sat a large waste tank, fuel tanks for the maneuvering jets and a heat radiator. Its pressurized volume, over 350 m³, was not matched until Mir was finished in 1996.

paragraphs.heading: Damaged on the way up
paragraphs.text: During launch the micrometeoroid shield tore off the workshop, ripping away one main solar array and jamming the other. That cost the station most of its electrical power and left it open to strong heating from the Sun, threatening to make it unusable. The first crew put up a replacement heat shade and freed the stuck panels, saving Skylab.

paragraphs.heading: Where the idea came from
paragraphs.text: Early champions of human spaceflight, such as rocket engineer Wernher von Braun and writer Arthur C. Clarke, expected until the 1960s that a station would be an important early step. In Collier's magazine between 1952 and 1954, von Braun helped describe a circular station 75 m across that would spin to make artificial gravity. Its 80 crew would include astronomers, weather forecasters and soldiers, and he expected trips to the Moon and Mars to leave from it. Later, uncrewed satellites could photograph weather and send the pictures to Earth, and Apollo picked a way to the Moon that needed no building in orbit. A smaller station that one rocket could launch still had value for science.

paragraphs.heading: Competing with the military
paragraphs.text: In September 1963 NASA and the Department of Defense agreed to build a station together. Yet in December the Defense Department announced its own Manned Orbiting Laboratory, a small station mainly for photo reconnaissance with large telescopes, run by a crew of two. For the next five years it competed with NASA's station for money. The military project pushed NASA to change its plans so they looked less like it.

paragraphs.heading: The end of Skylab
paragraphs.text: A follow-on station, Skylab B, was built in 1970 but cancelled in 1973. There were plans to use the Space Shuttle to boost Skylab higher and reuse it, but they were dropped once it was clear the shuttle would not be ready by 1979. Skylab's orbit gradually decayed, and on July 11, 1979, it broke up in the atmosphere, scattering debris over the Indian Ocean and Western Australia.
